title: Hypertension Teaching: Make the Home Plan Safer Than the Number
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Hypertension teaching should connect medication adherence, home BP technique, orthostasis/fall prevention, sodium and lifestyle goals, and urgent symptom recognition. A single elevated home reading is less important than the pattern plus symptoms and the prescribed escalation plan.
recognize: Poor cuff fit, talking, recent caffeine/exercise, pain and missed medicines can distort home readings.
Severe headache, chest pain, dyspnea, neurologic deficit or vision change with markedly elevated BP requires prompt escalation.
priorities: Reinforce correct home technique and medication schedule.
Teach the patient not to double missed doses unless specifically instructed.
Escalate severe symptoms or persistent extreme readings per the care plan.
assessMonitor: Trend BP log, orthostasis, adherence barriers, adverse effects and medication-reconciliation changes.
interventions: Reinforce standardized seated readings and follow-up rather than reacting to one isolated number.
medicationSafety: Review OTC decongestants, NSAIDs, stimulants and duplicate antihypertensive products that may worsen BP or adverse effects.
redFlags: Severe headache with neurologic or visual change
teaching: Bring the BP log and medication list to follow-up and know which symptoms require urgent care.
delegationScope: PNs may reinforce an established teaching plan and obtain/trend BP; new unstable findings or regimen changes require RN/provider involvement.
examTrap: Treating an asymptomatic single home reading as more important than symptoms, trend, technique and the prescribed escalation plan.
oneLinePearl: Teach the pattern, the medicines and the red flags—not just the target number.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. hypertension home-monitoring and medication-safety principles

title: Edema and Daily Weights: Catch Fluid Gain Before Breathing Worsens
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Daily weight is a sensitive home trend for fluid accumulation when measured consistently. The key is to interpret weight with edema, dyspnea, orthopnea, urine output and the patient-specific action plan rather than treating ankle swelling alone.
recognize: Rapid weight gain plus increasing dyspnea or orthopnea suggests worsening congestion.
Unilateral painful swelling is not routine heart-failure edema and requires evaluation for DVT or another local cause.
priorities: Use the same scale at about the same time under similar conditions.
Compare weight trend with respiratory symptoms and edema.
Escalate worsening dyspnea, hypoxemia, chest pain or rapid fluid accumulation per plan.
assessMonitor: Trend weight, edema location, lung symptoms, urine output, sodium/fluid plan and diuretic response.
interventions: Reinforce prescribed fluid/sodium guidance and medication adherence; do not independently increase diuretics unless the patient has an explicit clinician-directed plan.
medicationSafety: Extra diuretic dosing without an authorized plan can cause hypotension, kidney injury and electrolyte loss.
teaching: Record weights and symptoms together and follow the individualized call/urgent-care thresholds.
delegationScope: PNs may obtain/trend weights and reinforce the plan; interpretation of acute deterioration requires RN/provider escalation.
examTrap: Telling a patient to take extra diuretic solely because ankles look more swollen without checking the authorized plan and full clinical picture.
oneLinePearl: Weight is the early fluid alarm; breathing tells you how urgent it is.

title: COPD Home Care: Prevent the Exacerbation Spiral
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: COPD home care combines correct maintenance/rescue inhaler use, smoking cessation support, vaccination, activity/pulmonary-rehabilitation principles, nutrition and early recognition of exacerbation. Oxygen should be used exactly as prescribed, not increased indiscriminately for every episode of breathlessness.
recognize: Increasing dyspnea, sputum change, wheeze, falling activity tolerance or rescue-inhaler use can signal exacerbation.
New confusion, cyanosis, inability to speak full sentences or severe work of breathing indicates emergency deterioration.
priorities: Confirm inhaler technique and which medicine is rescue versus maintenance.
Reinforce the individualized exacerbation and oxygen plan.
Escalate severe respiratory distress, altered mental status or persistent hypoxemia.
assessMonitor: Trend baseline versus current dyspnea, sputum, oxygen use, inhaler adherence, activity, nutrition and infection symptoms.
interventions: Support pacing, pursed-lip breathing and prescribed pulmonary-rehabilitation/home-care strategies.
medicationSafety: Do not substitute repeated rescue bronchodilator use for evaluation of a worsening exacerbation; verify steroid/antibiotic action plans before use.
redFlags: Unable to maintain prescribed oxygen target
teaching: Know the rescue inhaler, maintenance inhalers, oxygen prescription and exact symptoms that trigger a call versus emergency care.
delegationScope: PNs may reinforce established home-care teaching and monitor response; acute respiratory decline requires escalation.
examTrap: Turning up oxygen without assessment simply because the patient feels more short of breath.
oneLinePearl: COPD home safety is early recognition plus correct rescue—not endless rescue.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. COPD management and oxygen-safety principles

title: Hypokalemia Symptoms: Weakness Can Become an Arrhythmia
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Hypokalemia may begin with fatigue, weakness, cramps or constipation but can progress to dangerous cardiac dysrhythmias, especially with digoxin exposure, diuretics, GI loss or concurrent hypomagnesemia.
recognize: Muscle weakness, cramps, ileus/constipation and palpitations are important cues.
ECG change, syncope or severe weakness raises urgency.
priorities: Identify ongoing losses and relevant medications.
Check magnesium and renal function when ordered because they affect safe correction.
Escalate dysrhythmia, severe weakness or ECG change.
assessMonitor: Trend potassium, magnesium, renal function, ECG/rhythm when indicated, GI losses and diuretic use.
interventions: Administer potassium replacement by the ordered route and concentration; never improvise IV concentration or rate.
medicationSafety: IV potassium must be diluted and pump-controlled according to policy; renal impairment increases overcorrection risk.
teaching: Report persistent vomiting/diarrhea, palpitations or marked weakness and follow the prescribed potassium plan.
delegationScope: PNs may monitor symptoms and administer ordered replacement within state/facility IV scope; rhythm instability requires immediate escalation.
examTrap: Treating a low potassium number without asking why it fell or whether magnesium/renal function changes correction safety.
oneLinePearl: Low potassium weakens muscle and destabilizes electricity.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. potassium replacement safety principles

title: PN Scope and Safety Basics: Stable, Predictable, Authorized
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: U.S. LPN/LVN practice is defined by state law plus employer policy and competence. On NCLEX-PN, the safest pattern is to perform authorized care for stable/predictable patients, collect focused data, reinforce established teaching, monitor response and promptly escalate new instability, diagnostic uncertainty or care-plan changes.
recognize: A sudden change in condition, new complex assessment need or unstable patient is not a routine assignment problem.
A task may be technically familiar but still unauthorized by the state, facility or patient-specific plan.
priorities: Check patient stability first, then task authorization and personal competence.
Clarify unclear assignments before proceeding.
Escalate acute change rather than independently redesigning the plan of care.
assessMonitor: Monitor for new instability, task-specific complications and whether the patient remains within the expected plan.
interventions: Use chain of command when an assignment appears unsafe or outside authorized scope.
medicationSafety: IV push, central-line, blood-product and specialty-medication authority varies by state/facility and must not be assumed.
teaching: Explain role boundaries clearly while ensuring the patient still receives timely care through the appropriate team member.
delegationScope: State law and employer policy govern; the PN remains accountable for accepting only authorized tasks and reporting changes promptly.
examTrap: Choosing a familiar procedure simply because the PN has done it before without checking patient stability and authorization.
oneLinePearl: Stable patient + authorized task + competence = safer PN assignment.

title: Vital-Sign Escalation: Trends Beat Isolated Numbers
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A vital sign matters most in context: baseline, trend, symptoms, medications and measurement quality. A newly abnormal pattern with clinical deterioration requires prompt reassessment and escalation even if no single number looks dramatic.
recognize: Rising respiratory rate, falling oxygen saturation, new tachycardia, hypotension, fever/hypothermia or altered mentation can precede collapse.
A technically suspect reading should be repeated correctly without delaying care when the patient looks ill.
priorities: Look at the patient first, verify the measurement, compare with trend and assess ABCs.
Escalate symptomatic or rapidly worsening abnormalities promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory rate, oxygenation, heart rate, BP, temperature, pain, mental status and urine output as appropriate.
interventions: Repeat measurements using correct equipment/technique and initiate ordered emergency/supportive measures while escalating.
medicationSafety: Consider opioids/sedatives, beta blockers, antihypertensives, antipyretics and other medicines that can alter the pattern or mask severity.
teaching: Home-monitoring patients should know when a symptom plus abnormal reading warrants urgent care rather than repeated checking.
delegationScope: Vital-sign collection may be delegated; interpretation and escalation of abnormal trends remain licensed-nurse responsibilities.
examTrap: Documenting a newly abnormal set of vital signs and waiting for the next scheduled round without reassessment.
oneLinePearl: A trend is a story; a single number is only one word.

title: Heart Failure Monitoring: Congestion, Perfusion, Response
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Heart-failure monitoring asks two questions repeatedly: is congestion worsening and is perfusion adequate? Weight, edema and lung symptoms must be interpreted with BP, mental status, urine output, renal function and medication response.
recognize: Increasing orthopnea, crackles, rapid weight gain and edema suggest congestion.
Cool skin, confusion, hypotension, oliguria or severe fatigue may indicate poor perfusion.
priorities: Compare current status with baseline and recent trend.
Escalate new resting dyspnea, hypoxemia, chest pain, syncope or poor perfusion.
assessMonitor: Trend weight, lung sounds, edema, oxygenation, BP/HR, urine output, renal function/electrolytes and medication response.
interventions: Administer ordered therapies, position for breathing comfort and reassess after interventions.
medicationSafety: Diuretics can worsen renal function/electrolytes; beta blockers and RAAS-modifying therapy require BP/HR/renal/potassium context.
teaching: Track weight and symptoms, take medicines as prescribed and use the individualized escalation plan.
delegationScope: PNs may monitor stable patients and reinforce teaching; acute decompensation requires RN/provider escalation.
examTrap: Focusing only on edema and missing hypotension, confusion and oliguria that suggest poor perfusion.
oneLinePearl: Heart failure is a balance problem: fluid backing up and blood not moving forward.

title: Oxygen Devices for PN Care: Match Device to Need and Reassess
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Oxygen is a medication: use the prescribed device/flow or target, verify equipment function, assess skin and humidification needs when applicable, and reassess the patient's response. Escalating oxygen requirement is a deterioration signal, not merely a device-adjustment problem.
recognize: Nasal cannula, simple mask, Venturi-type systems and higher-support devices deliver oxygen differently; patient condition determines appropriate support.
Falling saturation, increasing work of breathing or altered mentation despite oxygen requires urgent escalation.
priorities: Check patient, device fit, tubing, source and prescribed settings.
Reassess oxygenation and work of breathing after intervention.
Escalate rapidly increasing oxygen need or persistent hypoxemia.
assessMonitor: Trend SpO2, respiratory rate/effort, mental status, skin integrity, device tolerance and ordered target.
interventions: Maintain oxygen fire safety and avoid petroleum-based products around oxygen equipment.
medicationSafety: Do not apply a blanket high-flow strategy to every patient; follow the clinical target and escalation pathway.
teaching: No smoking/open flame around home oxygen; use only prescribed flow/settings unless an emergency plan states otherwise.
delegationScope: PN oxygen initiation/adjustment authority varies by state/facility and order sets; monitoring and escalation are always required.
examTrap: Treating a rising oxygen requirement as solved once the saturation number temporarily improves.
oneLinePearl: More oxygen needed = more illness until proven otherwise.

title: Insulin Administration Checks: Product, Glucose, Meal, Site, Safety
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Safe insulin administration requires verifying the exact insulin and concentration/device, current glucose and trend, timing relative to food or nutrition, dose/order, injection site and hypoglycemia risk. Site rotation and avoiding lipohypertrophy reduce erratic absorption.
recognize: Wrong insulin or concentration, delayed meals, interrupted tube feeds, renal decline or unplanned activity can create hypoglycemia.
Lipohypertrophy can cause unpredictable absorption and unexplained glucose variability.
priorities: Match insulin type to the ordered timing and nutrition plan.
Verify dose/concentration/device and current glucose.
Hold/clarify when nutrition or clinical status no longer matches the order rather than administering automatically.
assessMonitor: Trend glucose/CGM when available, meal or feed status, renal function context, injection sites and hypoglycemia symptoms.
interventions: Rotate sites, use the correct device and follow policy for independent checks of high-alert insulin products.
medicationSafety: Never assume pen/vial concentrations are interchangeable; do not share insulin pens between patients.
complications: DKA from omitted basal insulin in type 1 diabetes
teaching: Know the insulin name, purpose, timing, device and hypoglycemia rescue plan.
delegationScope: Insulin administration authority and double-check policy vary; PN must follow state/facility rules and escalate mismatched nutrition/order conditions.
examTrap: Giving rapid-acting insulin simply because it is scheduled when the meal or tube feeding has been unexpectedly delayed.
oneLinePearl: Before insulin: right product, right glucose, right food, right dose, right site.
sourceBasis: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026: insulin administration technique and hypoglycemia prevention

title: Oral Glucose-Lowering Drugs: Identify the Class Before Predicting the Risk
bottomLine: 'Oral hypoglycemics' are not one safety profile. Metformin, sulfonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, thiazolidinediones and alpha-glucosidase inhibitors differ in hypoglycemia risk, kidney considerations, heart-failure effects, infection/DKA risk and administration timing.
recognize: Sulfonylureas carry meaningful hypoglycemia risk; SGLT2 inhibitors can cause euglycemic DKA; pioglitazone can worsen fluid retention/heart failure.
DPP-4 inhibitors have product-specific renal-dosing differences; metformin safety changes with renal function and acute illness.
priorities: Identify the exact drug/class before teaching adverse effects or hold cues.
Review kidney function, hypoglycemia risk, acute illness/dehydration and heart-failure history where relevant.
assessMonitor: Trend glucose, renal function, volume status, infection symptoms, weight/edema and class-specific adverse effects.
interventions: Administer with the product-specific meal/timing instructions and reinforce sick-day/peri-procedure plans when prescribed.
medicationSafety: Do not combine a DPP-4 inhibitor with a GLP-1-based drug merely for extra glucose lowering; current ADA 2026 does not recommend the combination.
Do not infer safety from the word 'oral.'
redFlags: Persistent vomiting/abdominal pain with ketone concern
teaching: Know the medication class and its unique warning symptoms rather than memorizing one rule for all diabetes pills.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and reinforce established teaching; medication selection and regimen adjustment remain prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Assuming all oral diabetes drugs primarily cause hypoglycemia and missing class-specific emergencies.
oneLinePearl: Name the class before you name the danger.
sourceBasis: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 pharmacologic approaches
